en: The Sūtra on the Elephant Head Monastery Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vinītāśubha of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Elephant Head Monastery in the city of Gayā.

At that time, not long after the Tathāgata had attained Buddhahood, he was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus—all of whom had been rishis with spiral-topknots (śikhin) in past lives; they had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, long since departed from birth and death, exhausted all afflictions, possessed the wisdom of universal emptiness and the mind of meditative absorption, were fully awakened in all knowledge, had reached the other shore, and were all arhats. Furthermore, he was together with an immeasurable multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat alone in contemplation, entering various samādhis and surveying the entire dharma-realm. He realized for himself his attainment of the Way—possessing all-encompassing wisdom, having completed what was to be done, having laid down the heavy burdens, crossed the stream of birth and death, abandoned stinginess and greed, uprooted the thorns of the three poisons, exhausted all craving, assembled the great Dharma-ship, struck the great Dharma-drum, blew the great Dharma-conch, raised the great Dharma-banner, and severed the cycle of birth and death. He then proclaimed the True Dharma:
"I close the gates to the evil realms and open the doors to the paths of goodness; forever departing from impure lands, I travel through all pure realms."
When I contemplate those dharmas, who cultivates bodhi? Who attains bodhi? Who desires to attain it?
Among the past, present, and future, by whom is it realized?
"Is it attained by means of this body, or is it attained by means of the mind?
If it were attained by means of the body, this body is without cognition, just like grass, trees, sand, pebbles, walls, or screens—it possesses no awareness."

This body is a combination of the four great elements, born of father and mother; it constantly requires food and drink, clothing, bathing, and rubbing with oil, yet it ultimately ends in decay and destruction—it is a phenomenon subject to dissolution.

This bodhi is merely an empty name and lacks any substantial characteristic; it has no sound, no form, no accomplishment, no seeing, no entry, no cognition, no going, and no coming. Such dharmas as these are likewise without bondage.

It transcends all phenomena and surmounts the triple world; it is without seeing, without hearing, without self or what belongs to self, without an agent, without location, without a dwelling place, without grasping, without attachment, without exiting, without entering, without aspiration, without abiding, without marks, without features, without "that," without "this," and without demonstration—just like a magical illusion.

Arising through the twelve links of dependent origination, it has no location, is invisible, and is free from characteristics; it appears like space, is tranquil, and is without sound, resonance, pattern, letter, or verbal expression.
To know in this way is called bodhi.

If it were attained by means of the mind, that mind would have no fixed nature; it is like a magical illusion, all produced from the karma of past deluded thoughts, formless and ungraspable, just like empty space.
Bodhi has no location; it is neither past, nor future, nor present. All dharmas are empty.

Although they are expressed through speech, they have names but no reality. It is an unconditioned dharma—empty, signless, wishless, neither existent nor non-existent, not capable of being manifested, unspeakable, and inaudible.

Now, as for Bodhi: it is not attained in the past, not attained in the future, and not attained in the present; yet it is also not attained apart from the three periods of time. It is without marks, unconditioned, and not unconditioned. If one can thus awaken to and comprehend the dharmas of the three periods of time, that itself is Bodhi.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If non-characteristic (animitta) is awakening (bodhi), by what means do good sons and good daughters now abide so as to achieve awakening?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
“All bodhisattvas who train in awakening should abide in this manner.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should all bodhisattvas abide?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Now, Bodhi transcends the triple world, exceeds all verbal expression, is free from all letters and characters, and has no place of abiding. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in non-dwelling, this is dwelling in bodhi;
when they dwell in non-attachment, this is dwelling in bodhi;
when they dwell in empty dharmas, this is dwelling in bodhi.
To abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is to abide in bodhi;
to abide in the absence of intrinsic essence or characteristics in all phenomena is to abide in bodhi;
to abide in immeasurable faith is to abide in bodhi.
To abide without increase or decrease is to abide in bodhi;
to abide without divergent thoughts is to abide in bodhi;
to abide as being like a reflected image, like an echo in a valley, like the moon in water, and like a mirage in the heat, Mañjuśrī!
"To dwell in such dharmas as these is to dwell in bodhi.
At that time, the Devaputra Pure Radiant Flame addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How should one practice?"
"By what kind of karma does this bodhisattva practice? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
"To give rise to a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
The devaputra then addressed Mañjuśrī:
“How do the bodhisattvas practice so as to give rise to a mind of great compassion?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra! To be free from a mind of flattery and deception is the great loving-kindness of a bodhisattva."
The devaputra again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
“How should one practice to attain freedom from flattery and deception? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
To give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings is to be without flattery or deception; all bodhisattvas should train in this way.
The Son of Heaven then addressed Mañjuśrī again:
"How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice so as to give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings?
Mañjuśrī replied, "To be without 'that' and without 'this,' and to be free from all divergent views—this is the practice of equanimity; all bodhisattvas should train in this manner."
The devaputra again addressed Mañjuśrī:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva further cultivate the absence of ‘that’ and ‘this,’ the absence of various divergent views, and give rise to impartial conduct toward all sentient beings?”
Mañjuśrī said: "O Son of Heaven!
With virtuous mindfulness and reverence, being without 'that' or 'this,' without various divergent views, and regarding the dharma of equality—thus should all bodhisattvas practice."
The devaputra again addressed Mañjuśrī:
“By what cause does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful mindfulness and reverence arise—such that there is neither ‘that’ nor ‘this,’ and no various divergent views?”
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!
With wholesome mindfulness and reverence, one should give rise to the bodhicitta; all bodhisattvas should train in this manner."
The devaputra again addressed Mañjuśrī:
“From what cause does the bodhicitta arise? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! The bodhicitta arises from the six pāramitās.
The devaputra then addressed Mañjuśrī again:
“From where do the six pāramitās arise? Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!
"It arises from skillful means and wisdom.
The devaputra again addressed Mañjuśrī:
"From what do the skillful means and wisdom of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva arise?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra! Skillful means and wisdom arise from non-negligence."
The devaputra again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
“From what does non-heedlessness arise? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
Heedfulness arises from the cultivation of the three wholesome karmas.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“By what cause do the three wholesome karmas arise? Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!
"It arises from the cultivation of the ten wholesome courses of action.
The devaputra asked again,
"From what cause does the cultivation of the ten wholesome courses of action arise?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! It arises from the proper restraint of body, speech, and mind."
The devaputra asked Mañjuśrī again:
“From what do these three wholesome karmas arise? Mañjuśrī replied:
“It arises from right reflection.
The devaputra asked again:
“From what does right reflection arise?”
Mañjuśrī replied, “It arises from the practice of skillful contemplation.
The devaputra asked again:
“From what does the practice of skillful contemplation arise?
Mañjuśrī replied, “It arises from mindfulness and non-forgetfulness.”
The devaputra asked again:
"How many kinds of minds are there for recollecting and retaining [the teachings] without forgetting?
By what causes and conditions does one obtain the karmic fruit?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!
There are four kinds of arousal of the mind by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the fruit from its cause."
What are the four? First, the initial arousal of the mind; second, the cultivation of practice with focused mindfulness; third, non-retrogression; and fourth, being born together with the virtuous.
By means of the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment, one attains focused mindfulness;
by means of cultivating focused mindfulness, one attains non-retrogression;
and by means of non-retrogression, one is born together with the virtuous.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
One who has first resolved their mind is like sowing seeds in a fertile field;
the cultivation of practice with focused mindfulness is like the sprouting of seedlings."
The non-retrogression of their practice is like the growth of stems, trunks, branches, and leaves;
being born together with the good is like the formation and ripening of flowers and fruits.
The generation of the mind, the practice with focused mindfulness, non-retrogression, and being born together with the wholesome are likewise so.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A person who has first generated the mind is like a wheelwright, who well understands all kinds of wood."
To continue contemplating and practicing is like joining pieces of wood together;
to practice without regressing is like completing a chariot;
to be born together with the virtuous is like using it for transport.
The arousal of the mind, the continuous practice of recollection, non-retrogression, and being born together with the virtuous are likewise so.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
One who has first aroused the mind is like the new moon;"
Continuing to contemplate practice is like the moon on its fifth day, up to the seventh day;
practicing without regression is like the moon on its tenth day;
being born together with the wholesome is like the moon on its fourteenth day.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is complete and without deficiency, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
So too it is with the initial aspiration, the continuous recollection of practice, non-retrogression, and being born together with the virtuous.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra! One who has first resolved their mind upon enlightenment transcends the stage of the śrāvaka;
one who has resolved their mind for the second time transcends the stage of the pratyekabuddha."
The third arousal of the mind transcends the stage of non-fixation;
the fourth arousal of the mind attains the stage of fixation.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
Just as sounds such as *a* and *ā* are the root of all letters, so too is the initial arousal of the mind the root of all virtues;
just as by learning written characters one gains a small portion of knowledge, so too does the subsequent recollection and practice;
just as a mathematician, having gained a small portion of knowledge, calculates the infinite and knows its limits, so too is the mind of non-retrogression.
Knowing that the mind does not regress is like a person who clearly understands the sūtras and śāstras; being born together with goodness, their wholesome mind is likewise clear and lucid.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
The first arousal of the mind continues the contemplation of wholesome causes;
the second arousal of the mind continues the contemplation of wisdom;
the third arousal of the mind continues the contemplation of meditative concentration.
The fourth arousal of the mind continues the contemplation of the fruit.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
One who first arouses the mind upholds virtuous causes;..."
The second arousal of the mind involves upholding wisdom;
the third arousal of the mind involves upholding meditative concentration;
the fourth arousal of the mind involves upholding the fruit.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra! For one who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment], there is the accomplishment of wholesome causes;
for one who has resolved their mind a second time, there is the accomplishment of wisdom."
The third arousal of the mind achieves meditative concentration;
the fourth arousal of the mind achieves the true fruit.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
The first arousal of the mind enters the Way by means of goodness;
the second arousal of the mind enters the Way by means of wisdom;
the third arousal of the mind enters the Way by means of dhyāna.
The fourth arousal of the mind concerns entering the Path through cause and effect.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
one who first arouses the mind is like a physician who recognizes medicines;..."
The second arousal of the mind is skillfully knowing the medicinal ingredients;
the third arousal of the mind is administering medicine according to the illness;
the fourth arousal of the mind is causing them to take and apply it.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra! By virtue of the first production of the thought of enlightenment, one is born into the family of the Dharma King;
by the second production of the thought of enlightenment, one studies the Dharma of the Dharma King."
The third arousal of the mind is the practice of the conduct of the Dharma King;
the fourth arousal of the mind is the fulfillment of the royal station;
these are called the four kinds of arousal of the mind.
At that time, the Devaputra Pure Radiant Flame addressed Mañjuśrī:
“What is the swift path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
By practicing this path, the bodhisattva swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Mañjuśrī said: “O Devaputra!
There are two kinds of swift paths; by riding upon these two paths, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these two? First is the path of skillful means (upāyamārga), and second is the path of wisdom (prajñāmārga).
By upholding the knowledge of skillful means, one is able to contemplate all sentient beings.
By upholding the Prajñāpāramitā, one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena and is able to sever doubt and attachment.
By means of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), one brings all phenomena into harmony;
by means of Prajñā, all phenomena are not joined together.
Skillful means (upāya) is the cause, and wisdom (prajñā) is the fruit.
By means of skillful means, one knows all phenomena;
by means of wisdom, one knows that all phenomena are empty.
By means of the wisdom of skillful means, one adorns the Buddha-fields;
by means of prajñā, one knows that all Buddha-fields are entirely equal.
By means of skillful means, one knows the differences in the faculties and natures of all sentient beings.
By means of prajñā, one knows that the faculties and natures of all sentient beings are empty.
By means of upāya, one attains the flavor of the nectar of immortality and realizes bodhi;
by means of prajñā, one awakens to all Buddha-dharmas as the equal and correct path.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are two more practices that enable a bodhisattva mahāsattva to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
What are the two? First, the conditioned; second, the unconditioned.
The conditioned encompasses the five pāramitās in their entirety.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) comprehensively encompasses the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, there are two practices that enable a bodhisattva mahāsattva to swiftly attain awakening. What are these two?
First, there are contaminated practices; second, there are uncontaminated practices.
Contaminated practices refer to the five pāramitās;
uncontaminated practices refer to the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, there are two practices that enable a bodhisattva mahāsattva to swiftly attain awakening.
What are these two? First, the practice of abiding; second, the practice of non-abiding.
The practice of abiding consists of the five pāramitās;
the practice of non-abiding consists of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, there are two practices that enable a bodhisattva mahāsattva to swiftly attain bodhi.
What are these two? First, the measurable; second, the immeasurable.
The measurable refers to the five pāramitās;
The immeasurable is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Practice with measure is a dharma with signs (*sanimitta*);
practice without measure is a dharma without signs (*animitta*).
Furthermore, there are two practices that enable a bodhisattva mahāsattva to swiftly attain awakening.
What are these two? First, the practice of wisdom; second, the practice of meditative concentration.
"By means of the practice of wisdom, one proceeds from the first stage to the seventh;
by means of the practice of meditative concentration, one proceeds from the eighth stage to the tenth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Fearless Wisdom Dharani addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know meaning?
How does he know wisdom? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! Meaning has no substance, and wisdom likewise has no substance.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadramati, with fearless wisdom, again asked Mañjuśrī:
“How is it that when the object has no substance,
the cognition also has no substance? Mañjuśrī replied, “Good son!
That which is the essence-less meaning is unconditioned, uncreated, signless, formless, without coming, and without going; this is called "meaning.
That which is the essence-less wisdom is neither a fixed dharma nor a non-fixed dharma; this is called "wisdom.
One should receive and uphold it in this way.
Meaning has no essence; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Wisdom has an empty essence; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Without grasping and without abandoning—thus one should uphold this.
Furthermore, "meaning" is neither fixed nor non-fixed;
"wisdom" is called the path of the mind. When mind and wisdom are equal, there is no discrimination;
one should uphold it in this way.
Furthermore, the wise person takes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as their essence; concentration and wisdom are equal, without distinction.

By means of skillful means (*upāya*), they contemplate the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as they flow through birth and death, seeing the characteristics of good and evil as being like illusions and transformations—neither existent nor non-existent.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate all phenomena in this manner.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are ten further modes of wisdom-practice for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

What are the ten? First, the wisdom of causes; second, the wisdom of results; third, the wisdom of meaning; fourth, the wisdom of skillful means; fifth, the wisdom of *prajñā*; sixth, the wisdom of upholding and maintaining; seventh, the wisdom of the *pāramitās*; eighth, the wisdom of great compassion; ninth, the wisdom of pitying and teaching sentient beings; tenth, the wisdom of non-attachment to all phenomena.
These are called the ten kinds of wisdom-practices of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva undertakes ten kinds of pure practices."
What are the ten?

First, to personally initiate the practice of purity in physical action; second, to initiate the practice of purity in the physical actions of all sentient beings; third, to personally initiate the practice of purity in verbal action; fourth, to initiate the practice of purity in the verbal actions of all sentient beings; fifth, to personally initiate the practice of purity in mental action; sixth, to initiate the practice of purity in the mental actions of all sentient beings; seventh, to initiate the practice of pure equanimity toward all sentient beings; eighth, to initiate the practice of external pure equanimity toward all sentient beings; ninth, to initiate the practice of the pure wisdom of all Buddhas; tenth, to initiate the practice of purifying Buddha-lands and bringing sentient beings to maturity—furthermore, if there are sentient beings who encounter various illnesses, one shall provide them with medicine and medical care, enabling them to attain peace and happiness.
For those possessed of afflictions, he teaches and transforms them by means of unconditioned wisdom, causing them to leave the triple world;
he causes them all to be fully satisfied with the path of unconditioned merit and wisdom—this is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the ten kinds of pure conduct.
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva has ten kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). What are these ten?

First, the skillful means of reaching the other shore; second, the skillful means of upholding and maintaining; third, the skillful means of wisdom; fourth, the skillful means of skillful means; fifth, the skillful means of great compassion; sixth, the skillful means of fulfilling knowledge; seventh, the skillful means of fulfilling insight; eighth, the skillful means of tranquil mindfulness; ninth, the skillful means of true practice; tenth, the skillful means of equanimity toward all sentient beings, free from all hatred and attachment.
These are called the ten kinds of skillful means of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are ten kinds of inexhaustible differentiation of the body for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

What are the ten? First, the inexhaustible discernment of phenomena; second, the inexhaustible discernment of afflictions; third, the inexhaustible discernment of dharmas; fourth, the inexhaustible discernment of craving; fifth, the inexhaustible discernment of various views; sixth, the inexhaustible discernment of good and evil; seventh, the inexhaustible discernment of conditioned activities; eighth, the inexhaustible discernment of non-grasping and non-attachment; ninth, the inexhaustible discernment of harmonious integration; and tenth, the inexhaustible discernment of the perfection of bodhi-wisdom.
These are called the ten kinds of inexhaustible differentiation of the body. Furthermore, good son,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of practices for subduing.

What are these ten? First, the practice of subduing through virtuous conduct; second, the practice of subduing stinginess by giving gifts like rain; third, the practice of subduing lack of diligence; fourth, the practice of subduing the three karmas; fifth, the practice of subduing a poisonous mind by not becoming angry; sixth, the practice of subduing [the self] by giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion; seventh, the practice of subduing a lazy mind; eighth, the practice of subduing [the self] by diligently cultivating the Buddha-dharma; ninth, the practice of subduing unwholesome minds by not committing various evils; and tenth, the practice of subduing [the self] through mastery in meditative concentration and liberation.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of practices for subduing. What are the ten? First, the practice of subduing the breaking of ignorance and lack of wisdom;

second, the practice of subduing through the skillful means of upholding the *prajñāpāramitā*; third, the practice of subduing afflictions (*kleśa*); fourth, the practice of subduing the arising of the Path; fifth, the practice of subduing through the upholding of faith and realization; sixth, the practice of subduing so as not to fall into the evil realms; seventh, the practice of subduing unwholesome thoughts; eighth, the practice of subduing with mastery over the timely and the untimely; ninth, the practice of subduing one's own person; and tenth, the practice of subduing through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
These are called the ten kinds of practices for subduing. "Furthermore, good son,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten ways of subduing others.
What are these ten? They are:
the subduing and distancing oneself from the three evil karmas of body, the four evil karmas of speech, and the three evil karmas of mind.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of internal and external contemplation of phenomena, through which one does not give rise to attachment.
What are the ten? First, observing that the internal elements of the body are entirely empty, one does not give rise to attachment;
second, observing that the external elements of the body are also entirely empty, one does not give rise to attachment.
Third, observing that all internal and external phenomena are entirely empty, one does not give rise to attachment;
fourth, one does not give rise to attachment toward omniscience;
fifth, one does not give rise to attachment toward the path being practiced.
Sixth, observing the stages of the noble ones without giving rise to attachment;
seventh, practicing purity for a long time without giving rise to attachment;
eighth, abiding in the Prajñāpāramitā without giving rise to attachment.
Ninth, when teaching the Dharma through discourse to transform sentient beings, they do not give rise to attachment;
tenth, when observing all sentient beings, they give rise to great skillful means, compassion, and pity, yet do not give rise to attachment.
These are called the ten kinds of internal and external contemplation of phenomena that give rise to no attachment.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate a firm mind in this way while practicing the path to enlightenment."
If one does not thus possess such firm resolve for bodhi, one is not called a bodhisattva.
What is meant by "firm"?
When the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are in accord and do not contradict one another, this is called being firm.
What is meant by "not firm"?
When the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are not in accord and are mutually contradictory, this is called "not firm. Furthermore, good son:
Furthermore, there are two kinds of correct practice by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes the bodhicitta firm. What are these two?
First, the practice of right mindfulness toward bodhi; second, the practice of cultivating meditative concentration to sever all afflictions.
This is called the two kinds of firm bodhicitta through right practice.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are again two kinds of firmness in the right practice of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are these two? First, the cultivation of self-discipline in one's own physical conduct; second, the cultivation of discipline in the physical conduct of sentient beings. Good son!
This is called the two kinds of firmness in the correct practice of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, son of good family,
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have another two kinds of firmness in their correct practice.
What are these two?
First, attaining all-knowledge through diligent cultivation; second, attaining all-knowledge through non-cultivation.
This is called the two kinds of firmness in right practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are again two kinds of firmness in right practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What are these two? First, the firmness of correct practice through skillful means while abiding in the ground; second, the firmness of correct practice that is immovable while abiding in the ground.
These are called the two kinds of firmness of correct practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, good son, there are two other kinds of firmness in the correct practice of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these two?

First, the firmness of correct practice that remains far removed from defiled stages; second, the firmness of correct practice that brings one's own conduct to fulfillment through skillful means in each successive stage.
These are called the two kinds of firmness of correct practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further possess two kinds of firmness in right practice. What are these two?

First, the firmness of correct practice manifested in the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; second, the firmness of correct practice that does not regress from the skillful means toward the bodhi of a Buddha.
This is called the two kinds of firm correct practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. "Good son!
By means of such firmness in correct practice and immeasurable skillful means, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"Speak these words quickly!

When this Dharma was spoken, the entire great assembly—including Mañjuśrī, immeasurable devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—having heard the Buddha’s teaching, received it with faith, prostrated themselves, and joyfully practiced it.
The Elephant Head Monastery Sūtra (Hastikṣaṇa-vyākaraṇa-sūtra)
